summary.en: Use y-ordered merging and a narrow strip to find the closest planar pair in O(n log n) time.
summary.bn: y অনুযায়ী মার্জ ও মাঝের strip দিয়ে দ্রুত দুই নিকটতম বিন্দু খুঁজে বের করো।

notes: The Closest Pair of Points implementations use C17 and the numeric limits stated in their input contracts.

practice.title: Closest Pair of Points: justify the decisions
practice.statementHtml: Explain why the recurrence or decision rule for Closest Pair of Points covers every valid candidate, and why evaluation terminates.
practice.answerHtml:
Any optimal pair lies within a child slice or crosses the split. Recursive answers handle the within-child cases. For a crossing improvement over distance d, both endpoints lie in the strip and their vertical difference is below d. Thus scanning strip points in y order cannot miss an improving pair if it checks the relevant nearby successors.

The packing argument bounds those successors. Consider a strip window of width 2d and height d above a point. Its left and right half-windows each have width d. Subdivide each half into four squares of side d/2. Within one child slice, two points in one small square would be less than d apart, contradicting the child's minimum-distance bound.

There are at most eight occupied small squares across both sides, counting the starting point. Consequently at most seven later points need comparison. Boundary equality can be assigned consistently to neighbouring boxes; only pairs strictly closer than d matter. Points sharing the dividing x coordinate retain their child identity from the original split, so the same per-child separation argument applies.

If the best distance becomes zero, no smaller nonnegative distance exists. The strip tests may then admit no candidates, which is safe. The algorithm seeks the minimum value rather than all tied pairs. Counting every closest pair is a different output requirement and may require considering many duplicates.

Induction now completes correctness. Small slices are checked exhaustively. Larger slices return correct child values by assumption, merge y order correctly, and inspect every possible crossing improvement under the strip bound. The minimum of those cases is the global minimum. Each child is shorter, so recursion reaches a base.

practice.title: Closest Pair of Points: derive resource bounds
practice.statementHtml: Derive the time and auxiliary-space bounds for the implementations of Closest Pair of Points. Separate input, working storage and returned information.
hints: Duplicate coordinates make the minimum distance zero.
practice.answerHtml:
The initial x ordering costs O(n log n) with a comparison sort that guarantees that bound. At each recursive node, merging y orders takes Θ(n) work. Collecting the strip takes Θ(n), and at most seven comparisons per strip point add O(n). Thus T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n), giving Θ(n log n) recursive time.

The shared scratch array holds O(n) records. Active recursion adds O(log n) stack frames. This makes auxiliary space O(n), excluding the input records. Do not allocate a fresh n-element array in every live call without accounting for those allocations. Passing one reusable buffer keeps the memory argument tied to the implementation.

The C example uses qsort for the initial x ordering. C specifies its ordering behavior but does not guarantee a particular complexity. The O(n log n) algorithm bound assumes a suitable initial sorting routine, such as guaranteed merge sort. The closest routine itself has the stated recurrence independently of which correct initial sorter is chosen.

practice.statementHtml: Reproduce the worked Closest Pair of Points trace and explain each comparison or state change. State how the example handles equal candidates.
hints: Name the quantities in each row before making the next decision.
practice.answerHtml:
StageSquared boundReason
Left pair (0,0),(2,1)5Only two left points
Right minimum20(3,1) to (5,5)
Cross (2,1),(3,1)1Inside the strip
Final1No closer pair
StageSquared boundReason
Left pair (0,0),(2,1)5Only two left points
Right minimum20(3,1) to (5,5)
Cross (2,1),(3,1)1Inside the strip

The x-sorted root slices are [(0,0),(2,1)] and [(3,1),(5,5),(9,9)]. The left answer has squared distance 5, and the right answer is 20. The cross-boundary points (2,1) and (3,1) improve the result to 1. Solving only the two halves would therefore return the wrong value 5.

quiz.prompt: Why compare squared distances instead of distances?
options: It removes the need to subtract coordinates
quiz.explanation: Square root is increasing, so it is unnecessary for deciding the minimum.

quiz.prompt: What ordering must each closest call return?
options: Nondecreasing y order within its slice
quiz.explanation: The parent merges child y orders in linear time.
a[mid] may refer to a different point after child calls.

quiz.prompt: How many later strip neighbours suffice per point?
quiz.explanation: The packing argument bounds possible closer points in the vertical window.

quiz.prompt: What happens when two point records share coordinates?
quiz.explanation: Distinct records may coincide and form a zero-distance pair.

quiz.prompt: What cost results from sorting every strip afresh?
quiz.explanation: A logarithmic sort factor appears in the combine work at every level.

quiz.prompt: Why is n>=2 a public closest-pair precondition?
options: The array cannot hold one point
A singleton always has distance zero
One point has no distinct pair
qsort requires at least two records
quiz.explanation: Absence of a pair is different from a real zero-distance pair.

quiz.prompt: Does C guarantee qsort takes O(n log n) time?
options: No, its complexity is not specified
quiz.explanation: The theoretical presort bound assumes an appropriate sorting implementation.
Only the x coordinates differ by one.

quiz.prompt: How many unordered pairs does a five-point brute-force loop inspect?
Does a point at dx=3 enter a strict strip with squared bound 9?
quiz.explanation: Equality cannot improve the current distance, so the strict test is false.
